# **Academic Literature Review & Algorithmic Comparative Study for PCB Defect Inspection System (AOI)**

## **Comprehensive Critical Review of Prior Works**

[https://share.gemini.google/OXyCrRSMUh2F](https://share.gemini.google/OXyCrRSMUh2F)   
In the high-precision domain of electronic manufacturing, Automated Optical Inspection (AOI) represents a critical pillar of quality assurance pipelines1. As consumer demand drives the miniaturisation of electronic devices, printed circuit boards (PCBs) have evolved towards high-density interconnect (HDI) structures featuring sub-millimetre trace widths, microscopic vias, and tightly packed surface-mount technology (SMT) land pads4. Historically, quality control of bare PCBs relied on manual visual inspection, which has proven highly subjective, error-prone, and operationally inefficient7. Visual fatigue limits human defect detection rates to approximately 90% under magnification, a metric that collapses below 50% when multi-layered boards with high trace densities are evaluated7. Consequently, the development of contact-free, automated optical inspection systems has been essential for maintaining yield rates and minimizing industrial waste2.  
Over the past fifteen years, classical computer vision and digital image processing algorithms have dominated bare PCB inspection10. These methodologies are typically classified into three distinct paradigms: reference-based (template matching or subtraction), non-referential (design-rule checking), and hybrid approaches7. This literature review evaluates these techniques in the context of a comparative and enhancement study conducted for Tunku Abdul Rahman University of Management and Technology (TAR UMT), focusing on the benchmark Synthetic PCB Defect Dataset by Akhatova (derived from the Peking University Open Lab on Human-Robot Interaction)4. This dataset presents six physical defect types: missing holes, mouse bites, open circuits, shorts, spurs, and spurious copper4.

The evolution of image pre-processing in classical AOI systems exhibits a transition from global spatial filtering to adaptive, contrast-preserving enhancement10. Early inspection systems struggled with non-uniform surface reflections and lighting gradients5. The adoption of Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalisation (CLAHE) resolved many of these issues by partitioning the image into contextual tiles, performing local binarisation, and clipping the histogram to prevent over-saturation of copper trace edges15. Concurrently, spatial filters evolved from basic box car smoothing to Gaussian and Median filtering, which preserve critical edge transitions while suppressing high-frequency sensor noise8. Dynamic intensity mapping, implemented through operations such as IMadjust in MATLAB, further enhanced the contrast of bare boards prior to thresholding16.  
Image registration and alignment have transitioned from basic normalized cross-correlation (NCC) to local keypoint descriptor matching and perspective transformation10. Traditional NCC is highly effective for pure translational displacements, but fails when confronted with rotation, scale, or perspective shear17. The introduction of Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) and Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) enabled robust matching under geometric variations10. By matching localized invariant features across a test image and a reference template, and subsequently processing these matches via Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) to solve a homography matrix, modern AOI systems achieve precise spatial rectification10.  
Structural segmentation has advanced from global thresholding to adaptive, morphology-based decomposition10. Early attempts at pixel-level differencing were limited by binarisation artifacts along trace boundaries9. Putera (2010) introduced morphological image segmentation, dividing the PCB layout into primitive geometric regions (such as circular land pads, thin tracks, and broad bus bars) before applying comparison logic17. This segment-by-segment paradigm prevents noise propagation from highly textured areas into simple trace paths, significantly increasing classification accuracy24.  
Despite these developments, real-world operational environments continue to present significant challenges to classical PCB inspection systems2:

* **Micro-misalignment:** Sub-pixel translations and rotational skew, caused by mechanical positioning tolerances in high-speed optical conveyors, degrade pixel-level subtraction, producing false-positive edge rings9.  
* **Non-uniform illumination:** Bare copper surfaces exhibit highly specular reflections, whereas the surrounding glass-epoxy (FR-4) substrate acts as a matte absorber5. This contrast difference can distort global binarisation thresholds, causing the system to misidentify trace regions5.  
* **Chemical etching noise:** The chemical etching process naturally introduces micro-roughness along the boundaries of copper traces19. Rigid template subtraction systems frequently misclassify these acceptable tolerances as functional defects (such as mouse bites or spurs), raising the false-alarm rate25.  
* **Sub-pixel accuracy requirements:** Since defect sizes on high-density circuit boards can be as small as several microns, standard pixel-level grids are insufficient, necessitating sub-pixel interpolation algorithms in the spatial or frequency domains3.

## **Deep Dive into Five Image Processing Paradigms**

### **1\. Pixel-Level Direct Subtraction and Adaptive Binarisation**

Pixel-level direct subtraction relies on a rigid reference comparison mechanism12. Given a spatially aligned reference template image ![][image1] and a test board image ![][image2], the absolute difference image ![][image3] is computed16:  
![][image4]  
In practical implementations using library APIs such as OpenCV, this difference is extracted via cv2.absdiff32. To isolate directional deviations—such as excess copper versus missing copper—the subtraction is split into positive and negative difference channels to prevent negative values from wrapping or clipping under standard 8-bit unsigned integer constraints16:  
![][image5]  
![][image6]  
To suppress high-frequency sensor noise, the raw input images undergo spatial filtering8. Gaussian filtering applies a 2D isotropic convolution kernel to smooth the image9:  
![][image7]  
Alternatively, Median filtering acts as a non-linear operator, replacing each pixel value with the median intensity in its neighbourhood8. This is highly effective at eliminating impulsive salt-and-pepper noise while preserving the sharp structural transitions along copper trace edges8.  
Following noise reduction, adaptive binarisation is applied using Otsu's method, which selects an optimal threshold ![][image8] by maximizing the between-class variance of the grey-level histogram15. For an image with ![][image9] intensity levels ![][image10] and normalized histogram ![][image11], let a threshold ![][image12] divide the pixels into two classes: ![][image13] (background) and ![][image14] (foreground)37. The respective class probabilities ![][image15] and class means ![][image16] are calculated as follows37:  
![][image17]  
![][image18]  
The global mean is given by ![][image19]. The between-class variance ![][image20] is formulated as37:  
![][image21]  
The optimal binarisation threshold ![][image8] is defined as36:  
![][image22]  
While pixel-level direct subtraction is computationally efficient and highly suitable for locating gross surface deviations, it is extremely sensitive to minor spatial translations, scaling mismatches, and lighting fluctuations9. A spatial translation of even a single pixel along a high-frequency boundary creates an edge artifact, producing false-positive defect reports9.

### **2\. Frequency-Domain Analysis and Phase Correlation Registration**

Frequency-domain processing maps spatial details into spectral coefficients, separating structural copper trace patterns from global lighting variations16. The 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of an ![][image23] image ![][image24] is defined as40:  
![][image25]  
In the frequency domain, slow-varying global illumination changes correspond to low-frequency components clustered around the spectral origin ![][image26]16. Conversely, high-frequency components map to sharp edges, traces, and sensor noise16. Illumination invariance is achieved by applying a high-pass or band-pass homomorphic filter ![][image27], which suppresses low-frequency variations while preserving edge details16:  
![][image28]  
Phase correlation utilizes the shift theorem of the Fourier Transform to estimate the translation vector ![][image29] between a test board image ![][image30] and a reference template ![][image31] with sub-pixel precision19. If the test image is a translated version of the template, such that ![][image32], their Fourier Transforms satisfy19:  
![][image33]  
The cross-power spectrum ![][image34] is computed by multiplying ![][image35] by the complex conjugate of ![][image36], normalized by its magnitude31:  
![][image37]  
The Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform (IDFT) of this cross-power spectrum yields a spatial Dirac delta function31:  
![][image38]  
The spatial coordinates of the maximum peak in ![][image39] correspond to the translation offsets ![][image29]31. Sub-pixel precision is achieved by applying a 2D quadratic interpolation model over the ![][image40] pixel neighbourhood surrounding the peak, which enables accurate translation registration under varying light levels and minor noise conditions31.

### **3\. Structural Contour Analysis and Shape Descriptors**

Structural contour analysis characterises defects based on the geometric properties of their extracted boundaries10. This process begins with Canny edge detection, which uses Sobel operators to compute spatial gradients35. The gradient magnitude ![][image41] and orientation ![][image42] are defined as follows35:  
![][image43]  
Non-maximum suppression is applied along the gradient direction to thin these edges to single-pixel widths35. Hysteresis thresholding uses dual thresholds (![][image44]) to trace connected boundaries while suppressing isolated noise points35.  
Following boundary extraction, contours are organized into a nested hierarchy to model physical spatial relationships25. For each isolated contour, geometric features are extracted using Hu Moments, which provide scale, translation, and rotation invariance10. The 2D continuous raw moments ![][image45] and central moments ![][image46] of a digital image region ![][image24] are defined as38:  
![][image47]  
where ![][image48] and ![][image49] represent the centroid of the contour region38. Scale invariance is achieved by normalizing the central moments38:  
![][image50]  
Using these normalized central moments, the first two Hu Moments (![][image51]) are formulated as38:  
![][image52]  
![][image53]  
In addition, explicit geometric descriptors are extracted, including Aspect Ratio (![][image54]), Circularity (![][image55]), and Solidity (![][image56])25:  
![][image57]  
![][image58]  
![][image59]  
This paradigm is highly effective for isolating circular and geometrical anomalies such as *Missing Holes* and *Mouse Bites*4. A missing drill hole on a circular land pad is detected when the inner contour within the pad's hierarchy disappears, causing the calculated area of the inner loop to drop to zero25. Conversely, a mouse bite along a copper trace introduces a localized notch, which causes a sharp drop in trace solidity ![][image56] and circularity ![][image55] alongside a spike in high-order Hu moments due to the broken symmetry of the boundary line6.

### **4\. Morphological Filtering and Opening/Closing by Reconstruction**

Mathematical morphology analyzes spatial shapes by passing a structuring element ![][image60] of defined geometry (e.g., disc, line, or cross) over a binary image ![][image61]10. The fundamental operations are erosion (![][image62]) and dilation (![][image63])40:  
![][image64]  
![][image65]  
To isolate narrow features without altering the scale of the remaining structures, Top-Hat and Bottom-Hat transforms are employed23. The Top-Hat transform isolates bright elements smaller than the structuring element, whereas the Bottom-Hat transform isolates dark gaps40:  
![][image66]  
![][image67]  
where ![][image68] and ![][image69] represent morphological opening and closing, respectively40.  
To prevent shape distortion during noise filtering, Morphological Reconstruction is used22. This technique uses a "marker" image ![][image70] and a "mask" image ![][image71], where ![][image72]22. The geodesic dilation of size 1 of the marker ![][image70] with respect to the mask ![][image71] is defined as22:

The geodesic dilation of size ![][image74] is obtained by iteratively executing this operation until stability is reached, yielding the reconstruction ![][image75]22:

This paradigm is highly effective for isolating complex topological defects22:

* **Open Circuits:** An open circuit splits a trace into two disconnected segments4. By setting the marker ![][image70] as one end of the trace and the mask ![][image71] as the full trace template, morphological reconstruction will fail to traverse the break, leaving the disconnected segment un-reconstructed, which exposes the open circuit22.  
* **Shorts:** A short circuit creates an anomalous bridge connecting two distinct nets4. Applying an opening operation with a structuring element ![][image60] wider than the shorting bridge, followed by morphological reconstruction, eliminates the bridge while preserving the intact traces, isolating the short22.  
* **Spurs and Spurious Copper:** Spurs (protruding branch defects) are isolated by applying a hit-or-miss transform designed to detect line-end junctions on trace boundaries4. Spurious copper, which exists as isolated islands of copper, is extracted by performing a reconstruction utilizing a marker that avoids all legitimate nets; any foreground element that remains reconstructed is flagged as spurious copper4.

### **5\. Keypoint Feature-Based Alignment and Local Homography**

When a PCB test board exhibits rotational, scale, or perspective deformations relative to the reference template, simple translation alignment is insufficient19. Spatial alignment is achieved using keypoint feature detection coupled with projective homography10.  
The system detects scale-space local extrema using SIFT or ORB10. For SIFT, candidate keypoints are identified by searching for local extrema in the Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) space across multiple scales20:  
![][image77]  
For each validated keypoint, a local gradient orientation histogram is constructed to assign a dominant orientation, ensuring rotation invariance20. A 128-dimensional descriptor vector is then calculated to capture local gradient structures around the keypoint15.  
Feature vectors from the test image (![][image30]) and the template (![][image31]) are matched utilizing a Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN) matcher10. To eliminate ambiguous matches, Lowe's distance ratio test is applied, rejecting matches where the ratio of the distance to the nearest neighbour over the distance to the second-nearest neighbour exceeds 0.810.  
To calculate the global perspective mapping, outliers are rejected utilizing the Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) algorithm to solve the Homography matrix ![][image78]10. The projective homography matrix ![][image79] maps a point ![][image80] in the template to a point ![][image81] in the test board coordinate space21:  
![][image82]  
This matrix yields the inhomogeneous coordinate transformation21:  
![][image83]  
RANSAC iteratively selects random four-point correspondences, computes candidate ![][image78] matrices, and scores them by counting the number of inliers whose projective error falls below a predefined threshold ![][image84]10:  
![][image85]  
The homography matrix ![][image78] with the largest inlier count is selected21. Finally, a bilinear warp perspective interpolation is executed to warp the test board image into perfect spatial registration with the template, enabling edge-artifact-free pixel-level differencing19.

## **Master Literature Synthesis and Comparison Matrix**

Standard template differencing frequently fails in real-world industrial environments due to sub-pixel misalignment and uneven lighting9. To overcome these limitations, advanced AOI frameworks combine spatial registration (SIFT/FFT) with structural morphology and contour shape descriptors10. This multi-layered approach addresses the critical vulnerabilities of pixel-level differencing:

> 1. **Spatial Alignment Resolution:** Integrating SIFT or ORB homography transformations corrects for macro-level scale, rotation, and perspective shear introduced during board mounting or camera displacement10.  
> 2. **Sub-Pixel Jitter Cancellation:** While homography aligns the global coordinate system, localized board expansion or lens distortion introduces sub-pixel edge mismatches9. Incorporating frequency-domain Phase Correlation registration allows sub-pixel translation alignment down to ![][image86] pixels, suppressing false-positive edge rings in the difference image31.  
> 3. **Illumination and Etching Invariance:** Instead of directly subtracting raw pixel values, morphology-based binarisation (e.g., using top-hat transforms or geodesic reconstruction) and structural contour analysis (e.g., using Hu Moments and circularity) focus on geometric and topological properties22. These shape-based representations are invariant to lighting variations and minor etching tolerances, focusing on structural disconnections and bridges rather than cosmetic surface changes19.

The table below synthesises the landscape of classical optical inspection techniques developed over the past fifteen years, demonstrating how combining these paradigms addresses the weaknesses of standard template differencing.

## **Evaluation of the Proposed Comparative Study on the PKU Market Dataset**

To evaluate the proposed comparative framework, the system was tested on the Kaggle PCB Defects Dataset (PKU Market PCB / Synthetic PCB Defect Dataset by Akhatova)4. This dataset contains 1,386 high-resolution images generated via digital manipulation of bare boards, capturing six distinct physical defect types13:

> 1. **Missing Hole:** An omission of a drill hole within a circular pad4.  
> 2. **Mouse Bite:** A structural notch on the edge of a copper trace, representing localized erosion4.  
> 3. **Open Circuit:** A complete physical break in trace connectivity4.  
> 4. **Short:** An anomalous copper connection bridging two distinct trace nets4.  
> 5. **Spur:** A narrow copper protrusion branching off a legitimate trace boundary4.  
> 6. **Spurious Copper:** Isolated islands of copper debris scattered across the non-conductive substrate4.

The dataset exhibits highly challenging geometric characteristics, with defects often occupying only a small fraction of the image area, as documented in quantitative evaluations15:

| **Open Circuit** \[cite: 15\] | 16.13% (1,131 instances) | 2,674.74 | 0.05% |

For *Missing Holes*, the system extracts contour hierarchies, identifying nested circular loops25. When the inner pad contour vanishes and the circularity ![][image55] approaches 1.0 on the parent boundary, a missing drill hole is flagged25. For *Mouse Bites*, the local boundary profile is analyzed15. The defect causes a localized decrease in solidity ![][image56] and a high-order deviation in Hu moments, revealing the edge notch6.  
*Open Circuits* and *Shorts* are detected using Morphological Reconstruction22. An open circuit is flagged when geodesic dilation, initialized at a trace endpoint marker, fails to propagate across the entire trace mask, leaving the disconnected segment un-reconstructed22. Conversely, shorts are isolated by comparing the connected components of the binarised difference image22. A short creates an anomalous pathway that merges distinct nets, reducing the total connected component count while increasing the local Euler number22.  
*Spurs* and *Spurious Copper* are isolated using morphological hit-or-miss transforms and connected component filtering, which detect narrow copper protrusions and isolated copper islands on the substrate4. By matching specific algorithm designs to the geometric profiles of each defect, the proposed hybrid approach minimizes the false positives associated with standard pixel differencing under industrial inspection conditions19.
